procedural_history.impugned_order: Conviction and sentence under s. 302 read with s. 34, I.P.C.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Appeal to the Rajasthan High Court (Jaipur Bench) in Criminal Appeal No. 219 of 1977. The High Court maintained the conviction of the petitioner but acquitted his two associates.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The petitioner applied for special leave to appeal under Art. 136, which was dismissed. An application for review was also dismissed. Subsequently, the petitioner filed a petition under Art. 32, which the Supreme Court dismissed as not maintainable.

decision.appeal_result: the writ petition fails and is dismissed

issue.issue_text: Whether a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution is maintainable to challenge the legality of a conviction after a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 against the same conviction has been dismissed by the Supreme Court.

facts: A petitioner was convicted by a trial court and the conviction was upheld by the High Court.
The petitioner's Special Leave Petition (SLP) under Article 136 to the Supreme Court against the conviction was dismissed.
A subsequent application for review was also dismissed.

The petitioner then filed a writ petition under Article 32, arguing that his conviction was illegal and his resulting detention violated his fundamental rights under Article 21 (right to life and liberty).
law: Article 32 of the Constitution allows a person to approach the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of fundamental rights.
Article 136 of the Constitution grants the Supreme Court discretionary power to hear appeals from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal in India.
The principle of finality of judgments states that a decision made by the highest court is conclusive and cannot be re-agitated through different proceedings.
application: The Court held that the dismissal of the Special Leave Petition under Article 136 was a final judgment by the Supreme Court itself.
The Court reasoned that it would be improper to allow these proceedings under Article 32 to challenge a matter that the Court had already conclusively decided.
The petitioner's argument that his detention violated Article 21 was rejected because the detention resulted from a 'procedure established by law,' which included the final dismissal of his SLP.

Crucially, the Court stated that it cannot issue a writ to itself. The judges who dismissed the SLP constituted the Supreme Court for that matter, and they are not subject to the writ jurisdiction of the Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a writ petition under Article 32 is not maintainable to challenge the legality of a conviction after a Special Leave Petition against the same conviction has been dismissed. The dismissal of the SLP is a final judicial order of the Supreme Court, and the Court cannot issue a writ against its own final decision.

issue.issue_text: Whether the detention of a person in jail, following a conviction by the High Court and the subsequent dismissal of a Special Leave Petition by the Supreme Court, constitutes a deprivation of the fundamental right to life and liberty under Article 21, read with Articles 14 and 19.

facts: A petitioner was convicted by a trial court and the conviction was upheld by the High Court.
The petitioner then filed a Special Leave Petition (SLP) under Article 136 to appeal to the Supreme Court, but the petition was dismissed.

Subsequently, the petitioner filed a writ petition under Article 32 before the Supreme Court, arguing that his conviction was illegal and his resulting detention in jail violated his fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19, and 21.
law: A judgment delivered by a bench of the Supreme Court, including the dismissal of a Special Leave Petition, is final and cannot be overturned through a separate writ petition under Article 32.
The Supreme Court cannot issue a writ, direction, or order to itself in respect of its own judicial proceedings.
The judges constituting a bench of the Supreme Court are not amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the Court.
application: The Court found it improper for the petitioner to use an Article 32 petition to challenge the legality of his conviction, especially after the Court had already considered and dismissed his Special Leave Petition on the same matter.

The petitioner's detention was a result of a conviction that followed the 'procedure established by law,' which included the final step of the Supreme Court dismissing his SLP. Therefore, the detention could not be considered a violation of Article 21.

The Court reasoned that allowing such a petition would undermine the finality of its own judgments. The bench that dismissed the SLP constituted the Supreme Court, and its decision is final. Entertaining an Article 32 petition against that decision would be equivalent to the Court issuing a writ to itself, which is not permissible.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, holding that his detention did not violate his fundamental rights because it was the result of a lawful judicial process that had attained finality with the dismissal of his Special Leave Petition. A writ petition under Article 32 cannot be used to challenge a final judicial order of the Supreme Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court can issue a writ, direction, or order to itself in respect of its own judicial proceedings, such as the dismissal of a Special Leave Petition.

facts: A petitioner, whose conviction was upheld by the High Court, applied to the Supreme Court for a Special Leave Petition (SLP) under Article 136 of the Constitution.
The Supreme Court dismissed the SLP, and a subsequent application for review was also dismissed.

The petitioner then filed a new petition under Article 32 of the Constitution, asking the Supreme Court to issue a writ declaring his conviction illegal and his detention a violation of his fundamental rights.
This new petition effectively sought to overturn the finality of the Court's earlier decision to dismiss the SLP.
law: When judges are assigned to a Bench to hear a case, such as an SLP, they constitute the Supreme Court for that matter.
The judgments of the Supreme Court are final and cannot be upset by subsequent proceedings under Article 32.
The Supreme Court does not have writ jurisdiction over itself or the judges constituting its Benches in respect of their judicial proceedings.
The principle that a party cannot choose a second legal remedy to challenge an order after having already exhausted one remedy applies to proceedings in the Supreme Court.
application: The Court reasoned that the petitioner was attempting to use an Article 32 petition to challenge the same conviction that the Court had already refused to hear via the dismissal of his SLP under Article 136.
The Court held that the Bench which dismissed the SLP was, for that purpose, the Supreme Court, and its decision was final.
Allowing an Article 32 petition to challenge that final judicial order would mean the Supreme Court would be issuing a writ or direction to itself, which it cannot do.

The Court stated that the judges who made the decision are not amenable to the Court's own writ jurisdiction. To allow such a petition would be an abuse of process and would undermine the finality of the Court's decisions.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petition, holding that it cannot issue a writ, direction, or order to itself in respect of its own judicial proceedings. A decision by a Bench of the Court, such as the dismissal of a Special Leave Petition, is a final judgment that cannot be subsequently challenged or overturned through a new writ petition under Article 32.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution is maintainable to challenge the legality of a conviction after a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 against the same conviction has been dismissed by the Supreme Court.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner argued that since his Special Leave Petition (SLP) and a subsequent review application were dismissed, he had no other remedy except to approach the Court under Article 32.

He contended that the writ petition was maintainable to correct a grave injustice, as his conviction was illegal, and the dismissal of the SLP should not bar the court from exercising its jurisdiction to protect fundamental rights.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, as reflected in the court's judgment, is that such a petition is not maintainable.
The dismissal of a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 imparts finality to the judgment, which cannot be upset or circumvented by a subsequent writ petition under Article 32.
Allowing such a petition would be an improper exercise of discretion, especially after the petitioner has already chosen and exhausted the remedy under Article 136.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the detention of a person in jail, following a conviction by the High Court and the subsequent dismissal of a Special Leave Petition by the Supreme Court, constitutes a deprivation of the fundamental right to life and liberty under Article 21, read with Articles 14 and 19.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner argued that his conviction under s. 302 read with s. 34 IPC was illegal because his co-accused had been acquitted, citing previous Supreme Court decisions.

Based on this alleged illegality, he contended that his detention in jail was without the authority of law and therefore constituted a deprivation of his fundamental right to life and liberty under Article 21, read with Articles 14 and 19.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, as upheld by the court, is that the detention is lawful because it follows a conviction by a competent court and the subsequent dismissal of an SLP by the Supreme Court.
The detention is a result of following the 'procedure established by law', and therefore, it cannot be considered a violation of Article 21.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Supreme Court can issue a writ, direction, or order to itself in respect of its own judicial proceedings, such as the dismissal of a Special Leave Petition.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner sought a writ of mandamus directing the State to forbear from giving effect to the judgments of the lower courts as well as the Supreme Court's own order dismissing the Special Leave Petition.
This implicitly argues that the Court, under its Article 32 jurisdiction, has the power to issue orders that review and effectively nullify its own prior judicial orders.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, as articulated by the court, is that the Supreme Court cannot issue a writ, direction, or order to itself.
The judges constituting a bench are the Supreme Court, and they are not amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the Court.
Judicial proceedings of the Supreme Court have a finality and cannot be challenged through a writ petition directed at the Court itself.

cases.case_name: Shankar Ramchandra Abbyankar v. Krishnaji Dattatreya Bapat
cases.principle: When a party has chosen a specific legal remedy (like a revision petition under s. 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure) and that remedy has been exhausted and dismissed, it would not be a proper exercise of discretion for a court to grant relief in a different proceeding (like a writ petition under Arts. 226 and 227) challenging the same order. The Supreme Court applied this principle by analogy to hold that proceedings under Art. 32 should not be entertained after the Court has already declined to interfere under Art. 136.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A judgment of the Supreme Court, including an order dismissing a special leave petition under Article 136, is final and cannot be challenged or upset in subsequent proceedings under Article 32. The Supreme Court cannot issue a writ, direction, or order to itself in respect of its own judicial proceedings.
obiter: Where a party has chosen one of two alternative remedies and exhausted it, it would not be a proper and sound exercise of discretion for a court to grant relief in the other set of proceedings in respect of the same order of a subordinate court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution is not maintainable to challenge the legality of a conviction after a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 against the same conviction has been dismissed. The dismissal of the Special Leave Petition imparts a finality to the judgment which cannot be upset or circumvented by a subsequent writ petition, as the Supreme Court cannot issue a writ to itself in respect of its own judicial proceedings.
legal_tests_applied: The principle, derived from Shankar Ramclzandra Abbyankar v. Krishnaji Dattatreya Bapat, that once a party has chosen and exhausted one remedy (such as under Article 136), it would not be a proper and sound exercise of discretion for the court to grant relief in a different set of proceedings (such as under Article 32) in respect of the same underlying order.
why_appellant_lost: The petitioner's detention in jail does not amount to a deprivation of the fundamental right to life and liberty under Article 21, as it follows the 'procedure established by law,' namely a conviction by the High Court and the finality accorded to it by the Supreme Court's dismissal of the Special Leave Petition.

The Supreme Court cannot issue a writ, direction, or order to itself. The judges constituting a bench are the Supreme Court for the purpose of the case, and they are not amenable to the writ jurisdiction of the Court.

Having already chosen and exhausted the remedy under Article 136, the petitioner is barred from re-litigating the same issue through a writ petition under Article 32, as it would be an improper exercise of the court's discretion to entertain it.

The Court failed to appreciate the propriety of asking for a declaration under Article 32 that a conviction is illegal when the Court itself had already declined to grant special leave to appeal against that very conviction under Article 136.
why_respondent_won: The dismissal of a Special Leave Petition under Article 136 imparts finality to the lower court's judgment, and that finality cannot be upset by subsequent proceedings under Article 32.

The detention of the petitioner is lawful because it is a consequence of a conviction by a competent court, which has been upheld through the established appellate and discretionary review process, culminating in the dismissal of the SLP.
The Supreme Court lacks the jurisdiction to issue a writ to itself, as the judges sitting on a bench constitute the Supreme Court and are not subject to its writ jurisdiction.
policy_considerations: The court has an 'anxiety... to prevent abuse of process,' and allowing a party to challenge a final order through a different constitutional provision after exhausting one remedy would constitute such an abuse.
It is essential to 'respect and accord finality to its own decisions' to maintain the integrity and stability of the judicial system.
